h1:
Hat Yai Night Market Street Food
Greenway · Lee Gardens · ASEAN
intro: Night is when Hat Yai really comes alive for food. Once the sun drops, night markets open up across town one after another — from Greenway, a big open lot with everything in one place, to Lee Gardens Night Market, a long street you can graze down without stopping, all the way to the ASEAN Night Bazaar, where you can shop downstairs and eat at the upstairs food court in one trip. The headline eats here are grilled skewers, fried snacks and cold sweet treats — and they're all seriously cheap. We've sorted out which market is best for what, what's worth trying, the real opening hours, and a walking route so you don't end up circling the town in your car.

blocks.html: The charm of Hat Yai's night markets is that everything is piled into one spot. Walk a few steps and you go from smoky grills to hot fried snacks to Malay–Chinese–Thai sweets you'd struggle to find in other cities. Hat Yai is a border town where people of many backgrounds cross paths, so the flavors mix in fun ways. But each market has its own character — knowing that up front helps you pick the one that matches what you're craving and where you're staying that night.

blocks.text: Hat Yai's 3 main night markets, each strong at something different

items.name: Greenway Night Market
items.blurb: A big market lot on Kanchanawanit Road with a Greenway Food Station zone — a food court bringing together top stalls for savory dishes, sweets, grilled skewers and fried snacks, with comfortable seating. Open Tuesday–Sunday 5pm–10pm, closed Monday. Great for a full sit-down dinner.

items.name: Lee Gardens Night Market
items.blurb: A long street market in the city center, under 1 km from the train station. It opens around 4pm and is mostly a graze-as-you-go street food stretch, ideal for nibbling your way down and within walking distance of central-area hotels.

items.name: ASEAN Trade Bazaar (ASEAN Night Bazaar)
items.blurb: An open-stall market on Chotiwithayakul Road near Hat Yai's bus terminal. The building has two floors — clothing, shoes and secondhand finds downstairs, a multi-cuisine food court upstairs. Easy on the wallet, perfect if you like to shop and eat in one stop.
items.tag: Shop + eat · easy on the wallet

blocks.title: Check the day before you go
blocks.html: Greenway is closed every Monday, while Lee Gardens and ASEAN open almost daily but get busiest Friday–Saturday–Sunday. If you turn up on a Monday and still want a night market, head for Lee Gardens or ASEAN, since Greenway will be shut.

blocks.text: Hat Yai night market eats worth trying

blocks.html: We've ordered these by what comes up most often and what you can actually find in the main markets, leaning into the grilled, fried and sweet stuff that defines late-night street food here. The prices listed are rough ranges and will shift a bit depending on the stall and the size.

items.name: Grilled squid
items.blurb: The star of the grill at every Hat Yai night market. Fresh squid charcoal-grilled until fragrant, dipped in a punchy southern-style seafood sauce that's spicy, sour and loaded with garlic and chili. Greenway has several grilled-squid stalls to choose from, the smoke drifting toward you from a distance — order it with a cold beer or a fruit juice.
items.meta: Found at every market · best at Greenway

items.name: Grilled meatballs / grilled pork skewers
items.blurb: The snack you can't skip while you walk. Meatballs skewered and grilled until fragrant, brushed with a sweet-spicy sauce, while the pork skewers are milk-marinated and grilled soft — they pair perfectly with a small parcel of sticky rice. So cheap they're made for grabbing and grazing on the move before you reach your main-course stall.
items.meta: Every market · plenty at Lee Gardens

items.name: Salt-grilled fish / grilled prawns
items.blurb: A big grilled plate for the genuinely hungry. A whole fish packed in salt and grilled until the skin is crisp and the flesh stays juicy, picked apart and dipped in seafood sauce. Greenway has grilled-fish and grilled-seafood stalls where you can sit down for dinner — ideal when you come with a group and share.

items.name: Hat Yai fried chicken
items.blurb: The city's number-one fried snack, sold at plenty of night markets. Golden, crispy skin topped with a generous heap of fried shallots, eaten with hot sticky rice. Greenway has fried-chicken stalls to pick from — make it a main or a snack. If you want to zero in on the standout specialist shops, read on in our fried-chicken piece.

items.name: Mixed fried snacks — spring rolls, chicken rolls, fried tofu
items.blurb: Fried-snack stalls where everything's heaped out by the tray — fried spring rolls, chicken rolls, fried tofu, oyster omelet, even nuggets and assorted battered bits. Pick what you want into a bag and pay by the piece, then dip in plum sauce or sweet chili sauce. A hugely popular nibble while you walk the market.

items.name: Cart-style steak
items.blurb: Budget market-style steak that Hat Yai pulls off better than the price suggests. Beef, chicken or pork in black-pepper sauce, served with fries, corn and beans. Greenway has a well-known steak stall with a queue — one plate fills you up for just over a hundred baht. Perfect when you want something hearty without paying much.

items.name: Chicken rice / red barbecue pork rice
items.blurb: Chinese–Thai main-dish plates you'll find in the Greenway food court and the bigger markets. The chicken rice is soft and fragrant, drizzled with a bold fermented-soybean sauce — a dinner that genuinely fills you up. Good for anyone who doesn't want fried and grilled stuff all night and just wants a hot plate of rice.

items.name: Tokyo pancakes / Vietnamese rolled crepes
items.blurb: A favorite sweet you'll spot all across the night markets. Thin batter rolled around custard, sausage or various sweet fillings, made fresh and hot, and very cheap. Grab one to finish a meal or carry as you keep walking. Kids love them and adults happily munch along too.

items.name: Roti / banana-egg roti
items.blurb: A Malay–Muslim sweet that Hat Yai nails — buttery and fragrant, crisp outside and soft inside, fried fresh on the griddle with banana and egg, drizzled with condensed milk and dusted with sugar. A closing dessert that suits this town perfectly, found both in the markets and at roadside stalls around the late-night zone.
items.meta: Lee Gardens · roadside in the night zone

items.name: Cold sweets — bingsu, ice cream, shaved ice
items.blurb: Cap off a full belly with something cold to beat the heat — fluffy-ice bingsu, coconut-milk ice cream, shaved ice loaded with toppings. Greenway has several dessert and fresh-milk stalls to choose from, great for a rest before heading back, or to split after a heavy round of grilled food.

items.name: Fresh fruit juice / smoothies
items.blurb: The drink that pairs with a Hat Yai night market meal. Fresh-blended fruit juices and smoothies are something Greenway reviewers love to order — fresh and well-priced, cutting nicely through all the grilled and fried richness. There are also tea (cha chak), iced tea and herbal drink stalls to pick from as you like.
items.meta: Every market · several stalls at Greenway

items.name: Pork bone soup / hot brothy bowls
items.blurb: For a night when you want something hot to slurp, the Greenway food court has a big-pot pork-rib soup stall that locals order. The broth is rich and long-simmered, the meat falling off the bone and tender, eaten with steamed rice. A solid pick if you've walked yourself tired and want something warming.

blocks.title: Carry cash and small bills
blocks.html: Most market stalls take cash or PromptPay, but some small stalls can't scan easily when it's packed. Small bills make paying simpler, and keep in mind that a few popular stalls may sell out before closing if you arrive too late.

blocks.text: Make one night count — 2 routes by location

blocks.html: If you've only got one night and want to make it count, you don't need to hit every market. Pick a route based on where you're staying and the vibe you want. Here are two eating routes already mapped out for you.

blocks.label: Plan A
blocks.title: City-center grazer — Lee Gardens + roadside stalls

items.activity: Start at Lee Gardens Night Market
items.note: Walk over from a central-area hotel or near the train station. The market gets lively right about now.

items.activity: Graze the grills and fried snacks
items.note: Grilled pork, grilled meatballs, mixed fried snacks — one skewer, one piece at a time. Don't fill up at the first stall.
Chicken rice or fried chicken with sticky rice for a hearty course. Pick a stall with a moderate queue.
Hot banana-egg roti or Tokyo pancakes with a glass of blended fruit juice.

items.activity: Walk back / on to a late-night café
items.note: This area is an easy walk back to your hotel. If you're not sleepy yet, find a café to settle into.

blocks.label: Plan B
blocks.title: Sit-down and relax — Greenway as a full dinner

items.note: Take a ride or drive and park. The market opens at 5pm and is closed Monday. Go around now while everything's still stocked and it's not at peak crowds.
Grab a table first, then split up to order from several stalls and bring it all back to the table.

items.activity: Order grilled dishes as the star
items.note: Grilled squid, salt-grilled fish or grilled seafood. Add a cart-style steak if there's a group of you.

items.activity: Hot brothy bowl + a rice plate
items.note: Pork-rib soup or chicken rice to cut the richness, with a blended fruit juice.
Bingsu, coconut ice cream or fresh milk, then browse for gifts in the market before heading back.

blocks.title: Want shopping and eating in one go
blocks.html: If you want both shopping and food in a single spot, the ASEAN Night Bazaar fits the bill — browse clothes and shoes downstairs, then head up to the food court upstairs. Perfect for a night when you want to grab gifts and have dinner at the same time without moving on.

blocks.text: What to know before you go market-hopping

items: Opening hours — Greenway: Tuesday–Sunday 5pm–10pm, closed Monday · Lee Gardens: from around 4pm onward · ASEAN: evenings, almost daily. Check the venue's page first if you're going on a weekday.
When to go — around 6:00–7:30pm is the sweet spot: everything's stocked and it's not yet at peak crowds. Go late near closing and some stalls have sold out or are packing up.
Getting around — Lee Gardens is in the city center, walkable from many hotels · Greenway and ASEAN sit a bit outside the core, so a motorbike taxi, songthaew or Grab is easier.
Pace your appetite — there's so much food it's easy to fill up fast. Order a little from many stalls rather than a lot from one, so you can try more without filling up too soon.
Halal — Hat Yai has plenty of Muslim-run stalls, from grills to roti to main dishes. Look for the halal sign or just ask the stall — options are easy to find.

faq.q: Which Hat Yai night market is the best?
faq.a: It depends on what you're after. If you want to sit down comfortably with seating and a full spread of food, Greenway (open Tuesday–Sunday 5pm–10pm, closed Monday) is the standout. If you'd rather graze street food in the city center near your hotel, Lee Gardens Night Market does the job well. And anyone who wants to shop and eat in one place should head to the ASEAN Night Bazaar with its upstairs food court.

faq.q: What days and hours is Greenway Night Market in Hat Yai open?
faq.a: Greenway Night Market is open Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 5pm–10pm, and closed every Monday. It's on Kanchanawanit Road and has the Greenway Food Station food-court zone gathering lots of food stalls. We'd suggest going around 6:00–7:30pm, when everything's still stocked and it's not at peak crowds.

faq.q: What are the must-try eats at Hat Yai night markets?
faq.a: Grilled items like grilled squid, grilled meatballs, grilled pork skewers and salt-grilled fish, paired with fried things like Hat Yai fried chicken and mixed fried snacks. For sweets, go for Tokyo pancakes, banana-egg roti, and cold desserts like bingsu or shaved ice — then finish with a fresh blended fruit juice to cut the richness.

faq.q: What's the budget per person for a Hat Yai night market?
faq.a: Very easy on the wallet. Most snacks run 10–40 THB a plate, and a main like chicken rice or cart-style steak is around 40–120 THB. If you eat several things to really fill up, around 150–300 THB per person covers it — depending on how much grilled seafood you order.

faq.q: Do Hat Yai night markets have halal stalls?
faq.a: Plenty. Hat Yai has a large Muslim community, and many grill, roti and main-dish stalls are halal. Look for the halal sign at the front of the stall or just ask the vendor — there are easy options across Greenway, Lee Gardens and ASEAN.
